02 · Data plan: domains, datasets, periods and cost¶

Purpose of this notebook. Before any large download, this notebook fixes exactly what is downloaded (which regions, datasets and years) and tests every download on a short real sample, so that domains, periods, units and grids can be checked and the full cost estimated in advance.

How to read it. Every code cell has a short note above it saying what it does and why. Every figure has a caption underneath. The last section lists the design decisions this plan fixes, with the reason for each.

Sections

  1. The three analysis domains and the sub-regions
  2. Every dataset in the plan
  3. The paired experiments: observed and filtered sea-surface temperature
  4. A small real sample from every source (speed, size, units, values)
  5. Cost of the full download: time and disk space
  6. Sample maps: do the cut-outs line up?
  7. E-OBS station-based data
  8. Known issues
  9. Decisions fixed by this plan

What this cell does. Loads the project's own code from src/eerie_uk/. All the real work (opening data, cutting boxes, converting units, plotting) lives there, so the notebook stays short.

In [1]:
import sys, dataclasses, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, '../src')
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from eerie_uk import download as dl, plotting, regions

pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', 90, 'display.width', 220, 'display.float_format', '{:.2f}'.format)

1. Domains¶

The analysis works on three nested scales: the large-scale circulation (North Atlantic), the European response (north-west Europe), and the headline region (UK and Ireland).

What this cell does. Draws the three nested domains on one map, showing how much ocean and land each one covers.

In [2]:
domains = {name: regions.BOXES[name] for name in regions.DOMAINS}
plotting.plot_boxes(domains, regions.LABELS, title='The three analysis domains');

Figure 1. The North Atlantic box is used only for sea-level pressure (the NAO pattern). The north-west Europe box is what gets saved for temperature and precipitation. UK and Ireland is cut out of the north-west Europe files later; it needs no separate download.

What this cell does. Zooms in on north-west Europe and shows the three sub-regions used for headline numbers. The NAO makes the north wetter and the south drier (or the reverse), so one average over the whole box would cancel out; sub-regions keep that contrast visible.

In [3]:
inner = {name: regions.BOXES[name] for name in ('nw_europe',) + regions.SUBREGIONS}
plotting.plot_boxes(inner, regions.LABELS, title='North-west Europe and the proposed sub-regions');

Figure 2. UK and Ireland is the headline region. Western Norway and north-west France are my chosen as a wet northern and a drier southern counterpart. They can be moved without downloading anything again, because they are cut from the north-west Europe files.

What this cell does. Lists every box with its exact limits and its size in grid points on the 0.25° grid, so the numbers on the maps are also available as a table.

In [4]:
box_table = pd.DataFrame([
    {'box': regions.LABELS[name], 'code name': name,
     'west': b[0], 'east': b[1], 'south': b[2], 'north': b[3],
     'grid points (lat x lon)': f'{int((b[3]-b[2])/0.25)+1} x {int((b[1]-b[0])/0.25)+1}',
     'role': 'download' if name in ('north_atlantic', 'nw_europe') else 'cut from nw_europe later'}
    for name, b in regions.BOXES.items()])
box_table

2. Every dataset in the plan¶

The plan is defined in one place, eerie_uk.download.build_plan(). The downloader works through it in order: all monthly data first (small and quick), then daily data.

What this cell does. Prints the full plan: one row per download. server name is what the variable is called on the DKRZ server; saved as is the common name used in our files. coarsen = 4 means the field is averaged from 0.25° to 1° before saving (pressure only; the NAO is a basin-wide pattern and does not need 0.25°).

In [5]:
plan = dl.build_plan()
plan_table = pd.DataFrame([{
    'source': r.source, 'frequency': r.frequency, 'server name': r.native, 'saved as': r.variable,
    'period': f'{r.start_year}-{r.end_year}', 'box': r.box, 'coarsen': r.coarsen, 'dataset on DKRZ': r.dataset_id,
} for r in plan])
print(len(plan), 'downloads in the plan')
plan_table

Reading the table.

  • icon-esm-er and ifs-fesom2-sr are the two coupled EERIE models, historical run, member r1.
  • era5 is the observation-based reference (reanalysis), from the same DKRZ server.
  • ifs-amip-... are the paired atmosphere-only experiments explained in the next section.
  • Monthly model and ERA5 data cover 1950–2014; daily data cover 1985–2014; the paired experiments cover the years they exist, 1980–2023.

3. The paired experiments: observed and filtered sea-surface temperature¶

The descriptions of these runs come from the public EERIE intake catalogue on GitHub (dkrz/disk/model-output/ifs-amip-*/main.yaml):

Run What the catalogue says
ifs-amip-tco1279 . hist "high-resolution (tco1279, ~9 km) EERIE IFS-AMIP historical production run, forced with ESA-CCI v3 SST & sea ice"
ifs-amip-tco1279 . hist-c-0-a-lr20 the same, "filtered anomalies ... SST anomalies are filtered with LR20"
ifs-amip-tco399 . hist "medium-resolution (tco399, ~28 km)" version of the historical run
ifs-amip-tco399 . hist-c-0-a-lr20 medium-resolution run with filtered SST anomalies
ifs-amip-tco399 . hist-c-lr20-a-0 third medium-resolution variant; not described in the catalogue

What that means. These are atmosphere-only runs: the same atmosphere model, given observed sea-surface temperature in one run and a smoothed version (small-scale ocean features filtered out) in the other. That is a controlled test of the atmosphere's sensitivity to small-scale SST variability.

What the server provides. Monthly avg_msl (pressure), mean2t, mx2t, tprate on the 0.25° grid for 1980–2023. Daily mean temperature and precipitation exist, but daily maximum temperature does not on this grid. The ~28 km runs come as 10 members each, which is very valuable for a noisy quantity like the NAO.

Use in this project: monthly pressure for the NAO (notebook 07). Daily precipitation of the 9 km and 28 km historical runs is used later for the resolution comparison (notebook 08).

Two things not verified: exactly what the "LR20" filter is (presumably a low-pass spatial filter; the catalogue does not define it), and what hist-c-lr20-a-0 changes. The name suggests the filter is applied to the climatology instead of the anomalies. Both need the EERIE documentation before any result from these runs is interpreted.

4. A small real sample from every source¶

Before committing to hours of downloading, each of the downloads in the plan is tried on a short period: January–March 1990 for monthly data, 1–10 January 1990 for daily data.

What this cell does. Runs the short sample for every row of the plan, using exactly the same code path as the real download (open → cut to the box → convert units → save compressed netCDF). It records how long each time step took and how big the saved file is. This is the slowest cell in the notebook (a few minutes).

In [6]:
rows = []
for r in plan:
    start, end = ('1990-01-01', '1990-03-31T23:59:59') if r.frequency == 'mon' else ('1990-01-01', '1990-01-10T23:59:59')
    rows.append(dl.measure(r, start, end, '../data'))
samples = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(int(samples.ok.sum()), 'of', len(samples), 'samples succeeded')
samples[['source', 'frequency', 'variable', 'box', 'ok', 'error']]

5. Cost of the full download¶

The sample speeds are scaled up to the full periods. These are estimates: the server speed varies.

What this cell does. Multiplies the measured seconds-per-time-step and megabytes-per-time-step by the number of time steps in each full download, giving hours and gigabytes per row and in total.

In [8]:
cost_rows = []
for r, s in zip(plan, rows):
    if not s['ok']:
        continue
    c = dl.estimate(r, s['seconds_per_step'], s['mb_per_step'])
    cost_rows.append({'source': r.source, 'frequency': r.frequency, 'variable': r.variable, 'box': r.box,
                      'period': f'{r.start_year}-{r.end_year}', 'time steps': c['steps'],
                      'seconds per step': s['seconds_per_step'], 'hours': c['hours'], 'GB on disk': c['gb']})
cost = pd.DataFrame(cost_rows)
totals = cost.groupby('frequency')[['hours', 'GB on disk']].sum()
totals.loc['total'] = totals.sum()
print(totals.round(2).to_string())
cost

6. Sample maps: do the cut-outs line up?¶

The maps below are drawn from the sample files just saved. Free-running climate models do not reproduce the real weather of a given day or month, so the models and ERA5 are not expected to match in detail for January 1990. What should match is the region, the grid, the units and the general magnitude.

What this cell does. Defines a small helper that opens the saved sample files for one variable and returns one map per source (first time step; first member where a run has several).

In [11]:
def sample_maps(frequency, variable, reduce='first'):
    maps = {}
    for s in rows:
        if s['ok'] and s['frequency'] == frequency and s['variable'] == variable:
            field = xr.open_dataarray(s['path']).load()
            if 'realization' in field.dims:
                field = field.isel(realization=0)
            maps[s['source']] = field.isel(time=0) if reduce == 'first' else field.mean('time')
    return maps

What this cell does. Maps January 1990 mean sea-level pressure over the North Atlantic box for every source, on one shared colour scale. This is the field the NAO will be computed from.

In [12]:
plotting.plot_field_panels(sample_maps('mon', 'psl'), units='hPa', title='Monthly mean sea-level pressure, January 1990 (1° after coarsening)');

Figure 5. Every source shows the expected winter pattern: low pressure near Iceland, high pressure near the Azores. All panels cover the same box on the same 1° grid. For the 10-member runs only the first member is shown.

What this cell does. Maps January 1990 mean 2 m temperature over north-west Europe for the two coupled models and ERA5.

In [13]:
plotting.plot_field_panels(sample_maps('mon', 'tas'), units='K', title='Monthly mean 2 m temperature, January 1990');

Figure 6. Mild ocean, cold Scandinavia and Alps in all three. The ERA5 panel has been interpolated from ERA5's own grid to the same 0.25° grid as the models.

What this cell does. Maps January 1990 mean precipitation, after conversion to mm/day, to check that the three different server units ended up on the same scale.

In [14]:
plotting.plot_field_panels(sample_maps('mon', 'pr'), units='mm/day', title='Monthly mean precipitation, January 1990');

Figure 7. Similar magnitudes in all three sources, with the wettest values on west-facing coasts and mountains. If one unit conversion were wrong, that panel would be off by a factor of 1000 or 86 400 and would show as blank or saturated.

What this cell does. Maps daily precipitation averaged over the 10 sample days (1–10 January 1990), from the daily files. These are the data the precipitation extremes (RX1day, R95p) will be computed from.

In [15]:
plotting.plot_field_panels(sample_maps('day', 'pr', reduce='mean'), units='mm/day', title='Daily precipitation, mean of 1-10 January 1990');

Figure 8. Ten-day means from the daily data. The weather differs between panels because each model has its own storms; only the scale and the geography should agree.

What this cell does. The same for daily maximum temperature, the input for TXx.

In [16]:
plotting.plot_field_panels(sample_maps('day', 'tasmax', reduce='mean'), units='K', title='Daily maximum temperature, mean of 1-10 January 1990');

Figure 9. Ten-day mean of daily maximum temperature. Land–sea contrast and mountains appear in the same places in all three.

7. E-OBS station-based data¶

E-OBS is used as the land reference for extremes. It is distributed as two files:

File Content Size
rr_ens_mean_0.25deg_reg_v33.0e.nc daily precipitation, Europe, 0.25°, 1950 onwards 704 MB
tx_ens_mean_0.25deg_reg_v33.0e.nc daily maximum temperature, same grid 857 MB

Source: the ECA&D / Copernicus E-OBS access page (surfobs.climate.copernicus.eu). These are single files for the whole of Europe and the whole period, so about 1.6 GB to download in one go. They are cut to the north-west Europe box and the originals deleted (eerie_uk.eobs).

Terms of use. The data are "strictly for use in non-commercial research and non-commercial education projects" (ECA&D data policy). E-OBS is land-only, on the same 0.25° grid as the models, and is a more direct observation of extremes than ERA5, whose precipitation comes from a forecast model.

8. Known issues¶

  • Estimates, not guarantees. Download times come from samples of 3 time steps (monthly) or 10 (daily). The server was sometimes several times slower in earlier tests.
  • Connection drops. Short network failures (for example getaddrinfo failed) do occur. The downloader retries each year three times and skips years already saved, so a rerun simply continues.
  • ERA5 is interpolated. ERA5 is stored on its own grid (rows of different length); it is interpolated linearly to 0.25°. That slightly smooths sharp precipitation maxima.
  • ERA5 precipitation is a model product. It is not a direct observation. E-OBS would be the better reference for RX1day and R95p over land.
  • Time stamps differ. ICON-ESM-ER stamps a month at its end (31 January 23:59), IFS at mid-month, ERA5 at the first of the month. This is handled when years and seasons are selected, but it is a place where mistakes can hide, so notebook 03 checks it explicitly.
  • Model calendars are real calendars (with leap days), so no calendar conversion is needed.
  • Only member r1 of each coupled model is in the plan. Members r2 and r3 (1975–2014) exist and could be added for the NAO at small cost.
  • Paired experiments: the meaning of "LR20" and of hist-c-lr20-a-0 is not yet verified (section 3).
  • Later additions. Daily pressure (for notebook 09) and daily precipitation of the 9 km and 28 km atmosphere-only runs (for notebook 08) were added later, defined in eerie_uk.download.build_extension_plan(). To limit network traffic, the 28 km run uses its first three members and winter months only.

9. Decisions fixed by this plan¶

Decision Choice Reason
Domains North Atlantic 90°W–40°E, 20–80°N (pressure); north-west Europe 20°W–13°E, 40–65°N (temperature, precipitation); UK and Ireland 11°W–2.5°E, 49–61°N Large-scale circulation, European response, headline region (README, section 1)
Sub-regions UK and Ireland, western Norway, north-west France The two sides of the NAO rainfall see-saw around the headline region
Periods Monthly 1950–2014; daily 1985–2014; paired experiments 1980–2023 64 winters for the NAO; a standard 30-year period for extremes; the full span of the experiments
Sources ICON-ESM-ER r1, IFS-FESOM2-SR r1, ERA5, E-OBS, IFS atmosphere-only runs The only public EERIE runs with all fields needed (notebook 01)
Pressure resolution 1° instead of 0.25° Ample for the NAO, 16 times smaller on disk
Storage Compressed netCDF, one file per source, variable, region and year A failed download costs one year; reruns resume
